questions.question_text: Compared to cohort studies, case-control studies are typically:

options.text: Better for studying rare diseases or outcomes with long latency periods
Unable to establish temporal relationships between exposure and outcome

correct_answer.text: Better for studying rare diseases or outcomes with long latency periods

questions.explanation: While the source does not explicitly compare efficiency, case-control studies are fundamentally designed to work backward from outcome to exposure, making them ideal for rare outcomes and long-latency diseases. Case-control studies are analytical (hypothesis-testing), not merely descriptive. Option D is partially true but option C is the single best answer reflecting the practical advantage of case-control designs. Options A and E mischaracterize case-control studies. ---

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes why patient values and circumstances must be considered in EBM?

options.text: To ensure that evidence is applied in a manner relevant to individual patients' unique situations
To eliminate the need for clinical expertise
To prioritise patient preferences over clinical evidence

correct_answer.text: To ensure that evidence is applied in a manner relevant to individual patients' unique situations

questions.explanation: EBM's definition includes patient's unique values and circumstances as a core integrating component, and the Application step notes you will need to decide whether it can be applied to your patient

questions.question_text: A case vignette: A researcher plans to investigate the long-term outcome of early-onset schizophrenia in a cohort of 200 adolescents diagnosed in the past 2 years. She will follow them for 10 years. Which statement best describes the applicability of evidence from this cohort study?

options.text: The results can be immediately applied to all schizophrenia patients regardless of age or disease duration
The results are only applicable to early-onset cases within the first 2 years of diagnosis, and applicability must be assessed based on similarities to the clinician's patient population
Cohort studies cannot provide evidence for prognosis because they lack randomisation
The long follow-up period makes the study invalid for clinical practice
Results are generalisable only to adolescent males without comorbidities

correct_answer.text: The results are only applicable to early-onset cases within the first 2 years of diagnosis, and applicability must be assessed based on similarities to the clinician's patient population

questions.explanation: This reflects EBM Step 4 (Application) logic: the study population (early-onset, recent diagnosis, adolescents) defines the applicability boundaries. Clinicians must assess whether their patients match these criteria. Option A ignores population specificity. Option C is incorrect; cohort studies are ideal for prognosis. Option D falsely views follow-up duration negatively. Option E over-specifies generalisability limits. ---

questions.question_text: A clinician appraises a paper and finds it to have high internal validity and a clinically significant effect size, but the study population consisted exclusively of wealthy, white males aged 40–60 years. The clinician's patient is a 28-year-old woman from a low-income background. Which step of EBM is most relevant to this situation?

correct_answer.text: Application and assessing applicability

questions.explanation: The critical issue here is applicability—whether the valid and impactful results can be applied to this specific patient given differences in demographics, age, gender, and socioeconomic status. Step 4 (Application) explicitly requires assessing similarities and differences between study subjects and the individual patient before applying results. ---

questions.question_text: A case vignette: A psychiatrist identifies a novel adverse effect pattern in five patients treated with a new antipsychotic. She publishes this as a case series. What is the primary limitation of using this evidence for clinical decision-making?

options.text: Case series are too expensive and time-consuming to conduct
The observations are not generalisable to the broader patient population and are liable to selection, observation, and publication bias
Case series definitively establish causality between the drug and adverse effect
Case series are the highest level of evidence for safety monitoring
Case series eliminate all forms of clinical bias

correct_answer.text: The observations are not generalisable to the broader patient population and are liable to selection, observation, and publication bias

questions.explanation: The source identifies key limitations of case reports/series as Not generalisable and Liable for bias – selection

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the relationship between individual clinical expertise, external evidence, and patient values in evidence-based medicine?

options.text: External evidence should always override patient preferences
Clinical expertise is necessary but sufficient without external evidence
Integration of all three components is required for EBM
Patient values are least important in decision-making
External evidence is the only component required for valid EBM

correct_answer.text: Integration of all three components is required for EBM

questions.explanation: EBM requires the integration of individual clinical expertise, best available external evidence, and patient's unique values and circumstances. No single component is sufficient or should override the others. This integration is the defining characteristic of evidence-based medicine. ---

questions.question_text: An incomplete statement: Secondary research such as systematic reviews and meta-analyses tend to _____ results from different studies and provide _____ evidence for an intervention.

correct_answer.text: Summarise/integrate; the most reliable

questions.explanation: The source defines secondary research as studies that Tend to summarise / integrate results from different studies and Provide the most reliable evidence for an intervention. Options A (refute/lower-quality), B (inconsistent), D (criticise/expert), and E (exclude/preliminary) misrepresent the role of systematic reviews and meta-analyses as evidence synthesizers. ---

questions.question_text: An RCT of cognitive behavioural therapy for obsessive-compulsive disorder shows a 40% symptom reduction in the treatment group versus 15% in the control group. What does this finding primarily demonstrate about the study?

options.text: High validity and therefore definitive truth
Impact (clinically meaningful effect size) but validity requires additional appraisal
Both validity and applicability are confirmed
Results are automatically applicable to all patients

correct_answer.text: Impact (clinically meaningful effect size) but validity requires additional appraisal

questions.explanation: The large difference between groups (40% vs 15%) represents a substantial impact/effect size. However, validity (closeness to truth) requires appraisal of design quality, blinding, allocation concealment, loss to follow-up, and other biases. Large effect size alone doesn't guarantee validity. Applicability is a separate question requiring assessment of patient similarities. ---

questions.question_text: What is the primary advantage of qualitative studies compared to quantitative approaches?

options.text: They are always more reliable and valid
They are useful when conventional theories are inadequate to explain phenomena, such as why patients are non-concordant to medication
They eliminate all forms of bias
They are appropriate for all clinical questions

correct_answer.text: They are useful when conventional theories are inadequate to explain phenomena, such as why patients are non-concordant to medication

questions.explanation: The table states qualitative studies are useful when conventional theories are inadequate to explain

questions.question_text: A systematic review synthesises results from 20 different studies on the effectiveness of antidepressants for post-traumatic stress disorder. According to the hierarchy of evidence, what type of research is this?

options.text: Secondary research providing the most reliable evidence

correct_answer.text: Secondary research providing the most reliable evidence

questions.explanation: Secondary research (systematic reviews and meta-analyses) summarises and integrates results from different studies and provides the most reliable evidence for an intervention. This is distinct from primary research. Secondary research synthesises existing evidence rather than generating new data. ---

questions.question_text: A forest plot from a meta-analysis displays seven trials (Trials 1–7). Trial 1 has a square area of 0.05 cm², Trial 3 has 0.12 cm², Trial 4 has 0.09 cm², Trial 6 has 0.28 cm², and Trial 7 has 0.07 cm². Which trial has the greatest weight on the overall analysis?

correct_answer.text: Trial 6

questions.explanation: In a forest plot (blobbogram), the size of the square (blob) for each individual study represents its weight in the meta-analysis, which is proportional to its sample size or inverse variance The trial with the largest square contributes most to the pooled effect estimate. In the accompanying forest plot, Trial 6 has the largest square, indicating it has the greatest weight. Trials 1, 3, 4, and 7 have smaller squares and therefore contribute less to the pooled estimate.

questions.question_text: In the PICO framework for formulating clinical questions, what does the 'I' component represent?

options.text: Indicator, which may be diagnosis, prognosis, treatment or aetiology

correct_answer.text: Indicator, which may be diagnosis, prognosis, treatment or aetiology

questions.explanation: The source explicitly lists the four parts of a PICO question as Patient

questions.question_text: A researcher plans a study on the effectiveness of a new psychotherapy for anxiety but first wishes to understand patients' experiences and barriers to engagement. Which study design should be conducted FIRST according to the logic of research progression?

options.text: Qualitative study to generate hypotheses and understanding

correct_answer.text: Qualitative study to generate hypotheses and understanding

questions.explanation: Qualitative studies are suited for hypothesis generation when conventional understanding is inadequate, generating ideas that can be tested by subsequent quantitative research. Evidence demonstrates this progression—qualitative research first generates hypotheses and understanding, which are then tested by analytical and experimental studies. An RCT without preliminary qualitative understanding may miss important patient-centred barriers. --- **END OF 40 QUESTIONS**

questions.question_text: An incomplete statement: Analytical observational studies differ from descriptive observational studies in that they include _____ and are suitable for _____.

options.text: Comparison groups (cases/controls or cohorts) and controls; hypothesis testing
Large sample sizes; establishing definitive causality

correct_answer.text: Comparison groups (cases/controls or cohorts) and controls; hypothesis testing

questions.explanation: The source defines analytical observational studies as Comparison of two subject groups

questions.question_text: Cross-sectional studies are most appropriate when investigating:

options.text: Long-term prognosis of untreated psychiatric disorders
Causality between a risk factor and a psychiatric outcome
The value of screening or diagnostic tests and prevalence of disease
The efficacy of a new psychotropic medication
The aetiology of rare genetic psychiatric syndromes

correct_answer.text: The value of screening or diagnostic tests and prevalence of disease

questions.explanation: Evidence shows that cross-sectional studies are most appropriate when trying to answer questions concerning the value of screening or diagnostic tests and prevalence of a disease. Option B is wrong; cross-sectional studies identify association, not causality. Option A requires longitudinal follow-up. Option D requires an RCT. Option E is better suited to case reports or cohort studies. ---

questions.question_text: An RCT comparing an new antipsychotic to haloperidol in first-episode psychosis shows a statistically significant but small difference in negative symptom reduction (effect size d=0.15). Which aspect of critical appraisal does this primarily inform?

correct_answer.text: Impact (clinical significance of effect size)

questions.explanation: Impact refers to the size of the effect. While the result is statistically significant (related to validity), the small effect size (d=0.15) indicates limited clinical impact. This is an important distinction—statistical significance does not equal clinical significance. Applicability concerns patient relevance; validity concerns truthfulness of results. ---

questions.question_text: Which type of observational study design is most suitable for investigating whether childhood trauma is an aetiological factor in adult depression?

options.text: Case report of a single patient with childhood trauma and depression
Cross-sectional survey comparing depressed and non-depressed adults on childhood trauma history
Ecological study examining correlation between regional trauma rates and depression prevalence
Cohort or case-control study comparing trauma exposure and depression development
Clinical audit of current depression treatment protocols

correct_answer.text: Cohort or case-control study comparing trauma exposure and depression development

questions.explanation: The source's hierarchy indicates that for aetiology questions, cohort studies and case-control studies are appropriate. A case-control study could retrospectively assess trauma in depressed vs. non-depressed adults; a cohort study could prospectively follow trauma-exposed children. Option A (case report) is descriptive. Option B (cross-sectional) identifies association but not causality well. Option C (ecological) examines group-level patterns with fallacy risk. Option E (audit) assesses process, not aetiology. ---

questions.question_text: A meta-analysis of five high-quality RCTs investigating an antidepressant's efficacy would be classified as:

correct_answer.text: Level I evidence

questions.explanation: Level I evidence explicitly includes meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. A meta-analysis synthesising multiple RCTs represents the highest level of evidence hierarchy. Levels II, III, IV represent progressively lower evidence. Grade C corresponds to Level IV (expert opinion). The source clearly positions meta-analysis of RCTs at the apex of the evidence hierarchy.

questions.question_text: According to the evidence-based medicine framework, evaluation (Step 5) involves:

options.text: Assessing the clinician's effectiveness and efficiency in executing Steps 1-4 and seeking ways to improve them
Publishing all research findings regardless of quality
Accepting all expert committee recommendations without critical appraisal
Avoiding re-evaluation of clinical decisions once made
Restricting evidence use to published guidelines only

correct_answer.text: Assessing the clinician's effectiveness and efficiency in executing Steps 1-4 and seeking ways to improve them

questions.explanation: Evidence shows: This step is concerned with evaluating our effectiveness and efficiency in executing Steps 1-4 and seeking ways to improve them. This reflects a reflective, iterative approach to EBM practice. Options B (publication bias), C (expert-only), D (static practice), and E (guideline restriction) contradict the evaluative, self-reflective nature of Step 5. ---

questions.question_text: A qualitative study examining patient experiences of antipsychotic side effects shows that attitudes reported may not reflect actual behaviours. This illustrates which limitation of qualitative research?

correct_answer.text: Measurement bias and attitude-behaviour discordance

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that attitudes may not reflect behaviours and that information provided by participants may not reflect their actual behaviours—this is measurement bias and attitude-behaviour discordance. While generalisability is also a limitation, the specific discordance between reported and actual behaviour is the key issue. ---

questions.question_text: An incomplete statement: Descriptive observational studies are suitable for _____ rather than _____.

correct_answer.text: Hypothesis generation; hypothesis testing

questions.explanation: Evidence shows that descriptive observational studies Describes characteristics of a population and are Suitable for hypothesis generation rather than testing. Analytical and experimental studies are appropriate for hypothesis testing. Option A reverses the correct relationship. Options C, D, and E do not capture the hypothesis generation vs. testing distinction. ---

questions.question_text: A qualitative study found that patients with bipolar disorder report medication non-adherence due to perceived loss of creativity and emotional authenticity. According to the source, what is the most appropriate next step in the research cycle?

options.text: Publish the qualitative findings as definitive proof of non-adherence causality
Disregard the findings because qualitative research cannot be generalised
Use the hypothesis generated by this qualitative study as the basis for hypothesis testing through quantitative research
Immediately change clinical practice based on the qualitative findings without further evidence
Restrict the findings to the specific patient cohort and never apply them elsewhere

correct_answer.text: Use the hypothesis generated by this qualitative study as the basis for hypothesis testing through quantitative research

questions.explanation: The source explicitly describes qualitative studies' role: Generates hypothesis and ideas which can be tested by quantitative research. This reflects the iterative research cycle. Option A falsely claims causality from hypothesis generation. Option B contradicts the source's value attribution to qualitative research. Option D skips the hypothesis-testing phase. Option E over-restricts generalisability of hypothesis generation. ---

questions.question_text: A cohort study follows 500 men diagnosed with depression for 10 years, assessing the relationship between early life adversity and outcomes. Why might this study have limited applicability to clinical practice managing women with depression?

options.text: The study population differs in a relevant way (gender) from the target patient population
The follow-up period is too long
Depression outcomes are identical across genders

correct_answer.text: The study population differs in a relevant way (gender) from the target patient population

questions.explanation: Applicability assessment (Step 4) requires comparing study population characteristics to your patient. Men and women differ in depression presentation, course, treatment response, and outcomes; therefore, findings in an all-male cohort may not apply to women. This is a fundamental applicability issue. Sample size and follow-up duration are methodological concerns unrelated to applicability. ---

questions.question_text: An incomplete statement: RCTs are the ideal study design to assess _____ because they have _____ and can minimise _____.

options.text: Screening value; repeated measurement; selection bias
Causality and treatment effect; experimental and control groups; bias and confounding
Aetiology exclusively; observational structure; randomisation effects

correct_answer.text: Causality and treatment effect; experimental and control groups; bias and confounding

questions.explanation: The source defines experimental studies (including RCTs) as Ideal to assess causality / effect of treatment usually has two groups

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes why searching multiple databases, rather than relying on Medline/PubMed alone, is important when conducting a systematic review?

options.text: Medline/PubMed is biased toward negative studies
No single database, including Medline/PubMed, covers the full breadth of published scientific literature
Other databases have better statistical methodology
Multiple databases reduce, but do not eliminate, publication bias

correct_answer.text: No single database, including Medline/PubMed, covers the full breadth of published scientific literature

questions.explanation: According to the SPMM Course Notes (p.605), even a comprehensive multi-database search covers only 60–70% of the scientific literature, meaning no single database — including Medline/PubMed — provides anything close to complete coverage. This is why systematic reviews require searches across multiple databases, cross-checking reference lists, hand-searching, and contacting experts. Multiple databases reduce, but do not eliminate, publication bias. The other options are incorrect: Medline is not specifically biased toward negative studies; databases are repositories rather than methodological tools; and publication bias is not completely eliminated by using multiple databases.

questions.question_text: Which study design(s) are most appropriate for answering a clinical question about aetiology (causation)?

correct_answer.text: Cohort and case-control studies

questions.explanation: The hierarchy table explicitly lists RCT, cohort, and case-control as appropriate study designs for questions of aetiology. Cross-sectional and ecological studies are listed for other question types. While RCT is the gold standard, it is not the only appropriate design for aetiology questions, making RCT only incomplete. Ecological studies are not listed as suitable for aetiology.

questions.question_text: An incomplete statement: The critical appraisal process in EBM must evaluate the _____ of findings (methodological quality), the _____ of the effect (clinical meaningfulness), and the _____ to the clinician's patient population.

correct_answer.text: Validity; impact; applicability

questions.explanation: The source explicitly defines critical appraisal domains as assessing validity (closeness to the truth)

questions.question_text: Evidence-based medicine requires the integration of which three core components?

options.text: Clinical expertise, external evidence, and patient values
Clinical expertise, literature review, and cost analysis
Patient preference, randomised trials, and audit data
Expert opinion, case reports, and qualitative data

correct_answer.text: Clinical expertise, external evidence, and patient values

questions.explanation: EBM is explicitly defined as requiring integration of individual clinical expertise, best available external clinical evidence from systematic research, and patient's unique values and circumstances. Options B, C, D, and E omit or distort one of these three essential components. Cost analysis and cost-effectiveness are not mentioned as core EBM pillars. Expert opinion alone, without external evidence, contradicts the definition. Literature review is a method, not a core pillar.

questions.question_text: A major limitation of case reports and case series is that they are:

options.text: Not generalisable and liable to selection, observation, and publication bias
Unable to identify new clinical phenomena
Suitable only for hypothesis testing in psychiatric disorders
The highest level of evidence for treatment efficacy

correct_answer.text: Not generalisable and liable to selection, observation, and publication bias

questions.explanation: The source explicitly lists limitations of case reports/series as Not generalisable and Liable for bias – selection

questions.question_text: What is meant by applicability in the critical appraisal phase of evidence-based medicine?

options.text: Whether the study used appropriate statistical tests
The closeness of the results to the true effect
The usefulness of the evidence in your clinical practice
Whether the results are statistically significant
The ability to generalise to all populations worldwide

correct_answer.text: The usefulness of the evidence in your clinical practice

questions.explanation: Applicability refers to the usefulness of evidence in clinical practice—whether the study population, interventions, and outcomes are relevant to your patient. This is distinct from validity (closeness to truth) and impact (effect size). Applicability requires comparing study population characteristics to your own patient. ---

questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly identifies both a strength and a limitation of clinical audit?

options.text: Strength: cost-effectiveness; Limitation: inability to measure treatment outcomes
Strength: provides reliable estimates of effectiveness; Limitation: prone to all forms of bias
Strength: measures performance against criteria; Limitation: doesn't tell us how well they were done (effectiveness)
Strength: establishes causality; Limitation: lacks control groups
Strength: generalisable to all populations; Limitation: requires RCT comparison

correct_answer.text: Strength: measures performance against criteria; Limitation: doesn't tell us how well they were done (effectiveness)

questions.explanation: Evidence shows that audit Measures current performance against established standards/criteria (strength) but has the limitation: Because things have been done as per criteria

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist critically appraises a paper on antidepressant efficacy in geriatric depression. The study excluded patients over age 75, those with medical comorbidities, and those on polypharmacy. The psychiatrist's patient is a 79-year-old with diabetes and hypertension on three other medications. At which stage would this limitation become most relevant?

options.text: Application of results to the patient (assessing applicability)

correct_answer.text: Application of results to the patient (assessing applicability)

questions.explanation: The paper appears valid internally (the exclusion criteria may have been appropriate methodologically), but applicability is compromised because the patient differs substantially from the study population. Step 4 (Application) explicitly requires assessing similarities and differences between subjects in the paper and your patient before deciding whether results apply. ---

questions.question_text: A case vignette: A systematic review of 30 RCTs examining lithium efficacy in bipolar disorder finds consistent evidence of mood stabilisation across all included trials, with no significant heterogeneity. The review is published in a high-impact journal. According to the evidence hierarchy, what grade of recommendation should this evidence receive?

options.text: Grade C, because it is a summary of other studies
Grade A, because it comprises multiple RCTs of good quality and consistency without significant heterogeneity
Grade D, because some trials may have had small sample sizes
No grade, because systematic reviews are not part of the hierarchy

correct_answer.text: Grade A, because it comprises multiple RCTs of good quality and consistency without significant heterogeneity

questions.explanation: The source defines Grade A as At least one randomised controlled trial as part of a body of literature of overall good quality and consistency. A systematic review of 30 RCTs with consistent findings exemplifies this. The absence of significant heterogeneity supports Grade A classification. Options A (dismisses summary evidence), B (heterogeneity exists but is stated as minimal), D (small samples in individual trials do not negate aggregated evidence), and E (systematic reviews are secondary research providing highest evidence) are incorrect. ---

questions.question_text: In the hierarchy of evidence, where would a well-designed comparative descriptive study without randomisation be classified?

correct_answer.text: Level III

questions.explanation: Level III evidence includes well-designed non-experimental descriptive studies such as comparative studies and case studies. These lack randomisation and control groups. Level IIa includes controlled studies without randomisation; Level IIb includes quasi-experimental studies. Level I is RCTs/meta-analyses; Level IV is expert opinion. ---

questions.question_text: A researcher investigates why psychiatric patients are non-adherent to medications by interviewing them about their experiences and beliefs. Which research methodology is most appropriate?

correct_answer.text: Qualitative study

questions.explanation: Qualitative studies are described as useful when conventional theories are inadequate to explain

questions.question_text: A case vignette: A consultant psychiatrist reviews a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs examining selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) efficacy in major depression. The meta-analysis includes patients aged 18-75 with moderate-to-severe depression. The psychiatrist treats adolescent patients (aged 13-17) with mild depression. What is the key consideration in applying this evidence?

options.text: Meta-analyses are always generalisable to all age groups and severity levels
The evidence is invalid because the meta-analysis did not include adolescents and mild depression
The psychiatrist must assess the similarities and differences between the meta-analysis population and her adolescent, mild-depression patients before deciding applicability
Adolescent depression responds identically to adult depression; therefore, direct application is appropriate
The meta-analysis should be disregarded entirely in favour of case reports

correct_answer.text: The psychiatrist must assess the similarities and differences between the meta-analysis population and her adolescent, mild-depression patients before deciding applicability

questions.explanation: This scenario tests EBM Step 4 (applicability assessment). The source mandates: you will need to decide whether it can be applied to your patient

questions.question_text: An incomplete statement: Evidence obtained from well-designed non-experimental descriptive studies is classified as _____ on the hierarchy and receives a grade of _____.

correct_answer.text: Level III; Grade C

questions.explanation: The source explicitly defines Level III evidence as Evidence obtained from well-designed non-experimental descriptive studies

questions.question_text: Which type of bias is considered a particular methodological concern in qualitative research due to its reliance on non-standardised, observer-dependent data collection?

correct_answer.text: Observer bias

questions.explanation: Qualitative research relies on non-standardised data collection methods such as interviews and direct observation, making it particularly susceptible to observer bias (where the researcher\'s presence or interpretation influences findings) and measurement bias (due to absence of standardised, validated instruments). Selection bias, loss to follow-up, and recall bias are predominantly concerns in quantitative epidemiological study designs. Publication bias relates to dissemination rather than data collection methodology.

questions.question_text: Which database should be relied upon exclusively when searching for evidence in mental health research?

options.text: No single database should be used exclusively

correct_answer.text: No single database should be used exclusively

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that searching should not be restricted to one database like Medline/PubMed, which covers only 30–40% of published articles. Multiple databases should be searched to identify the best available evidence comprehensively. ---

questions.question_text: In a randomized double-blind trial two groups of hospitalized depressed individuals treated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are evaluated for benefi cial effects on insomnia of trazodone vs temazepam. Which of the following is NOT an significant factor when evaluating the internal validity of results obtained from the above study?

options.text: Baseline differences in antidepressant treatment between the two groups
The method used to randomize the sample
Setting in which the study takes place
Sensitivity of the insomnia scale to pick up changes in severity
Inclusion of the data in fi nal analysis from individuals who have dropped out

correct_answer.text: Setting in which the study takes place

questions.explanation: Threats to internal validity of an experimental study include confounding, selection bias, differential attrition, and quality of measurement. Having a signifi cant difference in baseline SSRI therapy could explain differential outcomes in the trazodone vs temazepam groups. Similarly, poor randomization may lead to selection bias and infl uence the differences in outcome. Failure to account for differential drop-out rates may spuriously infl ate or defl ate the difference in outcome. Using a scale with poor sensitivity to change will reduce the magnitude of differences that could be observed. Given both groups are recruited from the same setting (hospital), this must not infl uence validity; on the other hand, this might well infl uence generalizability of results to the non-hospitalized population (external validity) Campbell DT. Reforms as experiments. American Psychologist 1969; 24: 409–429. Slack MK and Draugalis JR. Establishing the internal and external validity of experimental studies. American Journal of Health-System Pharmacy 2001; 58: 2173–2181.

questions.question_text: A researcher is appraising a cross-sectional study investigating the prevalence of depression in primary care. Which feature would MOST limit the generalisability of this study?

options.text: Low response rate from volunteer bias

correct_answer.text: Low response rate from volunteer bias

questions.explanation: The cross-sectional study table explicitly states a key limitation is volunteer bias – as response rates can be very low and notes that the sample must be representative of the population – affects generalisability otherwise. This directly impacts external validity and generalisability. Small effect size affects clinical significance rather than generalisability. Lack of randomisation and absence of control group are features of descriptive designs by definition, not specific limitations to generalisability for cross-sectional studies.

questions.question_text: When a researcher searches for evidence in multiple databases rather than relying on Medline alone, what is the primary benefit?

options.text: Faster completion of the search process
Increased retrieval of published articles (beyond the ~30-40% in Medline)
Guaranteed finding of the best evidence
Reduction in time needed for critical appraisal

correct_answer.text: Increased retrieval of published articles (beyond the ~30-40% in Medline)

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states: It is important to have clear search terms and to search in different databases and not just restrict to one database like Medline (Pubmed)

questions.question_text: Which evidence level includes meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials?

correct_answer.text: Level I

questions.explanation: Level I evidence explicitly includes evidence obtained from a single randomised controlled trial or a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials addressing the specific recommendation. Meta-analysis represents the highest level of synthesis of RCT data. Levels II, III, and IV represent progressively lower levels of evidence. Level IIb refers to quasi-experimental studies.

questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of critical appraisal in the EBM process?

options.text: To ensure all studies are published in high-impact journals
To assess validity, impact, and applicability of searched evidence
To replace clinical expertise with research findings
To eliminate the need for patient input into decision-making
To guarantee that evidence applies to all patient populations

correct_answer.text: To assess validity, impact, and applicability of searched evidence

questions.explanation: Step 3 (Critical Appraisal) explicitly states it involves critically appraising that searched evidence for its validity (closeness to the truth)

questions.question_text: Which statement accurately reflects the relationship between study design selection and clinical question type?

options.text: All clinical questions are best answered by randomised controlled trials
The type of question determines the kind of study design most appropriate and leads to appropriate searching
Case reports are the most reliable source for answering questions about therapy or harm
Qualitative studies are never appropriate for clinical decision-making
The study design should be selected before formulating the clinical question

correct_answer.text: The type of question determines the kind of study design most appropriate and leads to appropriate searching

questions.explanation: Evidence shows: The type of question determines the kind of study design that is most appropriate and leads us to search appropriately. This reflects the logical sequence in EBM: question → design selection → search strategy. Option A is incorrect; different question types require different designs. Option C contradicts the hierarchy. Option D is false; qualitative studies have legitimate roles. Option E reverses the proper sequence. ---

questions.question_text: What is the primary advantage of secondary research (systematic reviews and meta-analyses) over individual primary studies?

options.text: They are quicker to conduct than RCTs
They integrate results from multiple studies and provide the most reliable evidence
They eliminate the need for primary research
They are less prone to publication bias

correct_answer.text: They integrate results from multiple studies and provide the most reliable evidence

questions.explanation: Secondary research explicitly provides the most reliable evidence for an intervention by summarising and integrating results across multiple studies. While systematic reviews may reduce some biases through comprehensive searching, publication bias can still occur. They do not eliminate the need for primary research but rather synthesise it. ---

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the ecological fallacy?

options.text: Environmental factors never affect psychiatric outcomes
Estimates of effect at the ecological level equate directly to individual-level biological effects
Estimates of effect at the ecological level do NOT equate to individual-level biological effects
Individual-level data are always more accurate than group-level data
Ecological studies are always invalid for clinical decision-making

correct_answer.text: Estimates of effect at the ecological level do NOT equate to individual-level biological effects

questions.explanation: The source explicitly defines the ecological fallacy limitation as: Estimates of effect at the ecological level do not equate to estimates of biological effect obtained from individual level analysis – ecological fallacy! Option B states the opposite (the fallacy itself). Options A, D, and E are overgeneralizations; ecological studies have value but are prone to this specific error. ---

questions.question_text: According to the evidence hierarchy, expert opinion alone without supporting clinical studies would be classified as:

correct_answer.text: Grade C evidence

questions.explanation: Table 1 explicitly defines Grade C as Expert committee reports or opinions and/or clinical experiences of respected authorities (evidence level IV). This grading indicates that directly applicable clinical studies of good quality are absent or not readily available. Expert opinion without supporting studies is Level IV/Grade C. Grades A and B require clinical trials or well-conducted studies. Levels I and IIa require RCT or controlled study data.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best defines evidence-based medicine?

options.text: The conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in patient care decisions integrated with clinical expertise and patient values
The application of randomised controlled trials to all clinical scenarios without exception
Adherence to expert opinion regardless of published research findings
The systematic use of clinical experience alone without reference to external evidence
The prioritisation of research evidence over individual patient circumstances

correct_answer.text: The conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in patient care decisions integrated with clinical expertise and patient values

questions.explanation: The source explicitly defines EBM as the conscientious

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes why a well-designed RCT might still have limited applicability despite high internal validity?

options.text: The sample size is too large
The control group was too similar to the treatment group
Strict inclusion/exclusion criteria create a study population unrepresentative of real-world patients
The effect size is statistically significant

questions.explanation: RCTs with strict inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., excluding comorbidities, age limits, polypharmacy) maintain high internal validity but reduce applicability to heterogeneous real-world populations. This is a common tension in RCT design. Randomisation reduces bias; statistical significance relates to validity; sample size and group similarity are methodological variables. ---

questions.question_text: Which study design is most appropriate for answering questions about the aetiology of a psychiatric disorder?

correct_answer.text: Cohort study or case-control study

questions.explanation: The best study designs for answering questions about causation (aetiology) are cohort studies or case-control studies. RCTs are reserved for treatment effectiveness and efficacy. Cross-sectional studies are most appropriate for diagnostic assessment or prevalence estimation. Case reports and ecological studies are descriptive designs that cannot establish causal associations. Therefore, \'cohort study or case-control study\' is the correct answer for aetiological questions.

questions.question_text: A clinician searches only Medline (PubMed) for evidence on antipsychotic efficacy. According to EBM literature search guidance, approximately what proportion of published scientific literature may be missed by a single-database search?

correct_answer.text: 30-40% missed (so 60-70% covered)

questions.explanation: Despite the availability of different databases, only 60-70% of scientific literature can be covered in a typical search. This means that restricting a search to a single database such as Medline (PubMed) risks missing approximately 30-40% of relevant studies. Options C, D, and E overestimate the proportion missed, while option A underestimates it. Searching multiple databases (e.g., Embase, PsycINFO, Cochrane) is therefore essential to minimise retrieval bias.

questions.question_text: What is the primary limitation of conducting a search in only one database such as Medline/PubMed?

It includes too many case reports

correct_answer.text: It will miss a significant proportion of relevant studies that are indexed only in other databases

questions.explanation: Searching only one database such as Medline/PubMed is a major methodological limitation in systematic reviews because it fails to capture studies indexed exclusively in other databases (e.g., Embase, PsycINFO, Cochrane, CINAHL, SIGLE). Best practice guidance recommends searching multiple databases to minimise retrieval bias and language bias. PubMed is free and widely used, so cost and time are not the primary limitations. Medline indexes peer-reviewed original research, not only expert opinions, and the volume of case reports is not the key concern. The core problem is incomplete coverage of the available literature.

questions.question_text: Zarkin et al., 2008 reported the cost-effectiveness comparison of naltrexone and placebo in alcohol abstinence. The mean effectiveness measured as percentage days of abstinence was nearly 80% for naltrexone group while it was 73% for the placebo group. The mean cost incurred for the placebo group was $400 per individual. The naltrexone group incurred a cost of 680 per individual. How much additional cost needs to be spent per individual for each percentage point increase in total days of abstinence when using naltrexone compared with placebo?
questions.explanation: The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER ) can be defi ned as the difference in AB cost (C) of interventions A and B divided by the difference in mean effectiveness (E), (C – C)/ A B (E – E), where intervention B is usually the placebo or standard intervention that is compared A B with intervention A. In this example, the difference in costs = $680 – 400 = $280. The difference in effectiveness as measured by percentage days of abstinence is 80 – 73% = 7%. Hence ICER = 280/7 = $40 per patient per percentage point of days of abstinence. Zarkin GA, Bray JW, Aldridge A, et al. Cost and cost-effectiveness of the COMBINE study in alcohol-dependent patients. Archives of General Psychiatry 2008; 65: 1214–1221.

questions.question_text: The effectiveness of an clinical measure is measured by using pragmatic trials. Which trial design is normally employed when carrying out a pragmatic trial?

correct_answer.text: RCT

questions.explanation: RCTs provide high-quality evidence for or against proposed interventions. But RCTs have a major limitation in terms of generalizability. This is because the trials are conducted in a somewhat artifi cial experimental setting that is different from clinical practice. So RCTs have high internal validity due to rigorous methodology but poor external validity. Pragmatic RCTs are a type of RCTs introduced with the intention of increasing external validity, i.e. generalizability of RCT results. But this takes place at the expense of internal validity. In pragmatic RCTs the trial takes place in a setting as close as possible to natural clinical practice, i.e. the inclusion and exclusion criteria are less fastidious, often ‘treatment as usual’ is employed for comparisons, instead of placebos and real world, functionally signifi cant outcomes are considered. Hotopf M. The pragmatic randomised controlled trial. Advances in Psychiatric Treatment 2002; 8: 326–333.
